blocks.text: Setting: The raised porch of Joe Clark’s Store and the street in front. Porch stretches almost completely across the stage, with a plank bench at either end. At the center of the porch three steps leading from street. Rear of porch, center, door to the store. On either side are single windows on which signs, at left, “Post Office,” and at right, “General Store” are painted. Soap boxes, axe handles, small kegs, etc., on porch on which townspeople sit and lounge during action. Above the roof of the porch the “false front,” or imitation second story of the shop is seen with large sign painted across it “Joe Clark’s General Store.” Large kerosene street lamp on post at right in front of porch.

Saturday afternoon and the villagers are gathered around the store. Several men sitting on boxes at edge of porch chewing sugarcane, spitting tobacco juice, arguing, some whittling, others eating peanuts. During the act the women all dressed up in starched dresses parade in and out of store. People buying groceries, kids playing in the street, etc. General noise of conversation, laughter and children shouting. But when the curtain rises there is momentary lull for cane-chewing. At left of porch four men are playing cards on a soap box, and seated on the edge of the porch at extreme right two children are engaged in a checker game, with the board on the floor between them.

When the curtain goes up the following characters are discovered on the porch: Mayor Joe Clark, the storekeeper; Deacon Hambo; Deacon Goodwin; Old Man Matt Brazzle; Will Cody; Sykes Jones; Lum Boger, the young town marshall; Lige Mosely and Walter Thomas, two village wags; Tom Nixon and Sam Mosely, and several others, seated on boxes, kegs, benches and floor of the porch. Tony Taylor is sitting on steps of porch with empty basket. Mrs. Taylor comes out with her arms full of groceries, empties them into basket and goes back in store. All the men are chewing sugarcane earnestly with varying facial expressions. The noise of the breaking and sucking of cane can be clearly heard in the silence. Occasionally the laughter and shouting of children is heard nearby off stage.
Yeah, and you ain’t got de chears in yo’ parlor you useter have.
Dat’s all right, Lige, but I betcha right now wid dese few teeth I got I kin eat up more cane’n you kin grow.
Off stage a high shrill voice can be heard calling:
I God, Jake Roberts buys mo’ rations out dis store than any man in dis town. I don’t see to my Maker whut she do wid it all.﻿ ﻿… Here she come.﻿ ﻿…
Aw gwan, Sister Roberts. You got plenty bacon home. Last week Jake bought.﻿ ﻿…
I God, woman, don’t keep on after me! Every time I look, youse round here beggin’ for everything you see.
And whut she don’t see she whoops for it just de same.
I God, naw! Yo’ husband done bought you plenty meat, nohow.
Sound of running feet inside the store.
Well, don’t touch it then. That’s all you’ll git outa me.
She reenters by door of store with the slab of meat in her hand and an outraged look on her face. She gazes all about her for sympathy.
She exits right on this line followed by the boy with the baby on his back.
All the men gaze behind her, then at each other and shake their heads.
Poor Jake.﻿ ﻿… I’m really sorry for dat man. If she was mine I’d beat her till her ears hung down like a Georgy mule.
I’d beat her till she smell like onions.
I’d romp on her till she slack like lime.
I’d stomp her till she rope like okra.
Well, did you git any partridges, Joe?
Resting his gun and seating himself.
Oh, the feathers flew off on de birds.
I don’t see nothin’ but dat bone. Look lak you done kilt a cow and et ’im raw out in de woods.
How you reckon we gointer know every hock-bone in Orange County sight unseen?
Standing the bone up on the floor of the porch.
General pleased interest. Everybody wants to touch it.
Takes bone in both hands and looks up and down the length of it.
he limps wid one hand on his buttocks
Dis mule was so evil he used to try to bite and kick when I’d go in de stable to feed ’im.
He was too mean to git fat. He was so skinny you could do a week’s washing on his ribs for a washboard and hang ’em up on his hipbones to dry.
He gets down on his back and illustrates.

I God, Brazzle, we all seen it. Didn’t we all go to de draggin’ out? More folks went to yo’ mule’s draggin’ out than went to last school closing.﻿ ﻿… Bet there ain’t been a thing right in mule-hell for four years.
Been dat long since he been dead?
I God, yes. He died de week after I started to cutting’ dat new ground.
The bone is passing from hand to hand. At last a boy about twelve takes it. He has just walked up and is proudly handling the bone when a woman’s voice is heard off stage right.
If you don’t come here you better!
He drops bone on ground down stage and trots off frowning.
Them girls done turned out to be right good-looking.
Teet ain’t as pretty now as she was a few years back. She used to be fat as a butterball wid legs just like two whiskey-kegs. She’s too skinny since she got her growth.
Ain’t none of ’em pretty as dat Miss Daisy. God! She’s pretty as a speckled pup.
But she was sho nuff ugly when she was little﻿ ﻿… little ole hard black knot. She sho has changed since she been away up North. If she ain’t pretty now, there ain’t a hound dog in Georgy.
Mist’ Clark, mama said is Daisy been here dis evenin’?
Ain’t laid my eyes on her. Ain’t she working over in Maitland?
Yessuh﻿ ﻿… but she’s off today and mama sent her down here to get de groceries.
Well, tell yo’ ma I ain’t seen her.
Well, she say to tell you when she come, to tell her ma say she better git home and dat quick.
Bet she’s off somewhere wid Dave or Jim.
I don’t bet it﻿ ﻿… I know it. She’s got them two in de go-long.
It’s lucky y’all girls done got some more fellers, cause look like Daisy done treed both Jim and Dave at once, or they done treed here one.
Let her have ’em﻿ ﻿… nobody don’t keer. They don’t handle de “In God we trust” lak my Johnson. He’s head bellman at de hotel.

Oh, I laks to see gals all mad. But dem boys is crazy sho nuff. Before Daisy come back here they both had a good-looking gal a piece. Now they ’bout to fall out and fight over half a gal a piece. Neither one won’t give over and let de other one have her.
Yeah, man. She handles a lot of traffic! Oh, mama, throw it in de river﻿ ﻿… papa’ll come git it!
Aw, shut up, you married men!
Senator been here long time ago hunting you.
She starts on in the store.
It’s powerful hot in dat store. Lemme run fetch ’em out to you.
He hurries on into the store.
Daisy, where’s yo’ two bodyguards? It don’t look natural to see you thout nary one of ’em.
Aw, don’ try to come dat over us, Daisy. You know who we talkin’ ’bout all right﻿ ﻿… but if you want me to come out flat-footed﻿ ﻿… where’s Jim and Dave?
Ain’t they playin’ somewhere for de white folks?

Yeah, but that’s ’bout all they do ’gree on these days. That’s de way it is wid men, young and old.﻿ ﻿… I don’t keer how long they been friends and how thick they been﻿ ﻿… a woman kin come between ’em. David and Jonather never would have been friends so long if Jonather had of been any great hand wid de wimmen. You ain’t never seen no two roosters that likes one another.
I ain’t tried to break ’em up.
All the men watch her out of sight in silence.
I God, a great big mango﻿ ﻿… a sweet smell, you know, with a strong flavor, but not something you could mash up like a strawberry. Something with a body to it.
He rises sullenly and goes inside the store.
Say, Hambo, I didn’t see you at our Sunday School picnic.

Looka here, Hambo. Y’all Baptist carry dis close-communion business too far. If a person ain’t half drownded in de lake and half et up by alligators, y’all think he ain’t baptized, so you can’t take communion wid him. Now I reckon you can’t even drink lemonade and eat chicken perlow wid us.
Well, I went to de Baptist picnic wid my mouf all set to eat chicken, when lo and behold y’all had chitlings! Do Jesus!
Hold on there a minute. There was plenty chicken at dat picnic, which I do know is right.

Only chicken I seen was half a chicken yo’ pastor musta tried to swaller whole cause he was choked stiff as a board when I come long﻿ ﻿… wid de whole deacon’s board beating him in de back, trying to knock it out his throat.

Say, dat puts me in de mind of a Baptist brother that was crazy ’bout de preachers and de preacher was crazy ’bout feeding his face. So his son got tired of trying to beat dese stump-knockers to de grub on the table, so one day he throwed out some slams ’bout dese preachers. Dat made his old man mad, so he tole his son to git out. He boy ast him “Where must I go, papa?” He says, “Go on to hell I reckon﻿ ﻿… I don’t keer where you go.”

So de boy left and was gone seven years. He come back one cold, windy night and rapped on de door. “Who dat?” de old man ast him. “It’s me, Jack.” De old man opened de door, so glad to see his son agin, and tole Jack to come in. He did and looked all round de place. Seven or eight preachers was sitting round de fire eatin’ and drinkin’.
“Where you been all dis time, Jack?” de old man ast him.
“I been to hell,” Jack tole him.
“Tell us how it is down there, Jack.”
“Well,” he says, “It’s just like it is here﻿ ﻿… you cain’t git to de fire for de preachers.”
Boy, you kin lie just like de crossties from Jacksonville to Key West. De presidin’ elder must come round on his circuit teaching y’all how to tell ’em, cause you couldn’t lie dat good just natural.
Can’t nobody beat Baptist folks lying﻿ ﻿… and I ain’t never found out how come you think youse so important.
Ain’t we got de finest and de biggest church? Macedonia Baptist will hold more folks than any two buildings in town.
Thass right, y’all got a heap more church than you got members to go in it.
Thass all right﻿ ﻿… y’all ain’t got neither de church nor de members. Everything that’s had in this town got to be held in our church.
Come on out, Tush Hawg, lemme beat you some checkers. I’m tired of fending and proving wid dese boys ain’t got no hair on they chest yet.
I God, you mean you gointer get beat. You can’t handle me﻿ ﻿… I’m a tush hawg.
To two small boys using checkerboard on edge of porch.
The children go down stage and call out:
Hey, Senator. Hey, Marthy. Come on let’s play chick-me, chick-me, cranie-crow.
I God! Hambo, you can’t play no checkers.
As they seat themselves at the checkerboard.
The children get louder and louder, drowning out the men’s voices.
And I’m gointer be de hawk. Lemme git maself a stick to mark wid.
The boy who is the hawk squats center stage with a short twig in his hand. The largest girl lines up the other children behind her.
The march around the hawk commences.
Chick mah chick mah craney crow Went to de well to wash ma toe When I come back ma chick was gone What time, ole witch?
Making a tally on the ground.
Can be repeated any number of times.
He rises and imitates a hawk flying and trying to catch a chicken. Calling in a high voice:
Flapping wings to protect her young.
During all this the hawk is feinting and darting in his efforts to catch a chicken, and the chickens are dancing defensively, the hen trying to protect them.
At the checkerboard, his voice rising above the noise of the playing children, slapping his sides jubilantly.
Don’t see how he can beat the Mayor like that.
Why’nt you go on away from here, Matilda? Didn’t you hear me tell you-all to move?
You impudent little huzzy, you! You must smell yourself﻿ ﻿… youse so fresh.
The wind musta changed and you smell your own top lip.
Don’t make me have to grab you and take you down a buttonhole lower.
Laughing to the scale and jumping a checker each time.
Oh, ha! Done got the ol’ tush hog.
Thought you couldn’t be beat, Brother Mayor?
Peeved, gets up and goes into the store mumbling.
Eh, heh.﻿ ﻿… Hambo done run him on his store﻿ ﻿… done run the ol’ coon in his hole.
That ain’t good politics, Hambo, beatin’ the Mayor.
Well, Hambo, you don’t got to be so hard at checkers, come on let’s see what you can do with de cards. Lum Boger there got his hands full nursin’ the chilluns.

Ya all can’t play no Florida Flip. When I was a sinner there wasn’t a man in this state could beat me playin’ that game. But I’m a deacon in Macedonia Baptist now and I don’t bother with the cards no more.
To man with basket on steps.
On opposite side of porch from card game.
Ain’t I tole you little Haitians to stay away from here?
De Mayor say for you to go round in de backyard and tie up old lady Jackson’s mule what’s trampin’ aup all de tomatoes in my garden.
Yawning and putting down the deck of cards.
Naw, they ain’t been here today. You-all know they ain’t so thick nohow as they was since Daisy Bailey come back and they started runnin’ after her.
You mean since she started runnin’ after them, the young hussy.
He begins shuffling the cards with an elaborate fan-shape movement.
Look out there, Lige, you shuffling mighty lot. Don’t carry the cub to us.
Didn’t snatch that jack, did you?
Aw, no, ain’t snatched no jack. Play.
Play jus’ like I’m in New York, partner. But we gotta try to catch that jack.
I’m playin’ a diamond for you, partner.
I done tole you you ain’t got no partner.
When that trick is turned, triumphantly:
Stands on his feet and slams down with his ace violently.
Everybody plays and the hand is ended.
Get up off your knees. Go ahead and tell ’em I sent you.
Pulls a quarter out of his pocket and lays it down on the box.
What you want me to play for you partner?
Takes the jack of diamonds and sticks him up on his forehead. Stands up on his feet.
He slams down the ace of diamonds. Pats the jack on his forehead, sings:
Gimme them cards﻿ ﻿… lemme deal some.
Frank, now you really got responsibility on you. They’s got one game on us.
Aw, you snatched that ace, nigger.
Yeah, they done carried the cub to us, partner.
Oh, he didn’t do no such a thing. That ace was turned fair. We jus’ too hard for you﻿ ﻿… we eats our dinner out a the blacksmith shop.
Aw, you all cheatin’. You know it wasn’t fair.
Scared to play you? Get back down to this table, let me spread my mess.
Yonder comes Elder Simms. You all better squat that rabbit. They’ll be having you all up in the church for playin’ cards.
How do, children. Right warm for this time in November, ain’t it?
Yes sir, Reverend, sho is. How’s Sister Simms?
Goes on in store with his children.

She look jus’ as good as you-all’s Baptist pastor’s wife. Pshaw, you ain’t seen no big woman, nohow, man. I seen one once so big she went to whip her little boy and he run up under her belly and hid six months ’fore she could find him.
Well, I knowed a woman so little that she had to get up on a soap box to look over a grain of sand.
The two children start primly off down the street but just out of sight one of them utters a loud cry.
I told you to go on and leave them other children alone.
You all varmints leave them nice chillun alone.
How big, you say it was, Frank?
Maybe not quite as big as that, but jus’ about fourteen feet.
Well, I don’t know about that. Some of the snakes around here is powerful long. I went out in my front yard yesterday right after the rain and killed a great big ol’ cottonmouth.
Well, the Mayor ain’t said nothin’ ’bout it.
When the folks misbehaves in this town I think they oughta lock ’em up in a jail and make ’em work their fine out on the streets, then these weeds would be cut down.
How we gonna do that when we ain’t got no jail?
Well, you sho needs a jail﻿ ﻿… you-all needs a whole lot of improvements round this town. I ain’t never pastored no town so way-back as this one here.
Who has lately emerged from the store, fanning himself, overhears this last remark and bristles up.
I say we needs some improvements here in this town﻿ ﻿… that’s what.

A whole heap. Now, for one thing we really does need a jail, Mayor. We oughta stop runnin’ these people out of town that misbehaves, and lock ’em up. Others towns has jails, everytown I ever pastored had a jail. Don’t see how come we can’t have one.
Well, there ain’t no sense in no one man stayin’ Mayor all the time.
Well, it’s my town and I can be mayor jus’ as long as I want to. It was me that put this town on the map.
What map you put it on, Joe Clark? I ain’t seen it on no map.
His remarks are drowned out by the others.
happening to notice the street light
Don’t you-all fuss now. How come you two always yam-yamming at each other?
Turns and sees wife standing in door. Commandingly.
White folks needs jails. We colored folks don’t need no jail.
Yes, we do, too. Elder Simms is right.﻿ ﻿…
The argument becomes a hubbub of voices.
Emerging from the store door, arms full of groceries, looking at her husband.

Two carelessly dressed, happy-go-lucky fellows enter together. One is fingering a guitar without playing any particular tune, and the other has his hat cocked over his eyes in a burlesque, dude-like manner. There are casual greetings.
How did you-all make out this evenin’, boys?
Oh, them white folks at the party shelled out right well. Kept Dave busy pickin’ it up. How much did we make today, Dave?
She sho is lookin’ stylish and pretty since she come back with her white folks from up North. Wearin’ the swellest clothes. And that coal-black hair of hers jus’ won’t quit.
Well, she always did look like new money to me when she was here before.
Well, that’s all you ever did get was a look.
That’s all you know! I bet I get more than that now.
You might git it but I’m the man to use it. I’m a bottom fish.
Aw, man. You musta been walking round here fast asleep when Daisy was in this county last. You ain’t seen de go I had with her.
No, I ain’t seen it. Bet you didn’t have no letter from her while she been away.
Well, it’s just cause she can’t write. If she knew how to scratch with a pencil I’d had a ton of ’em.
Shaw, man! I’d had a post office full of ’em.

You-all ought to be shame, carrying on over a brazen heifer like Daisy Taylor. Jus’ cause she’s been up North and come back, I reckon you cutting de fool sho ’nough now. She ain’t studying none of you-all nohow. All she wants is what you got in your pocket.
I likes her but she won’t git nothin’ outa me. She never did. I wouldn’t give a poor consumpted cripple crab a crutch to cross the River Jurdon.
I know I ain’t gonna give no woman nothin’. I wouldn’t give a dog a doughnut if he treed a terrapin.
Youse a cottontail dispute﻿ ﻿… both of you. You’d give her anything you got. You’d give her Georgia with a fence ’round it.
Yeah, and she’d take it, too.
Don’t distriminate the woman like that. That ain’t nothing but hogism. Ain’t nothin’ the matter with Daisy, she’s all right.
No, we ain’t. We’se come to get our mail.
Aw, who thinkin’ ’bout marryin’ now? They better stay home and eat their own pa’s rations. I gotta buy myself some shoes.
The woman I’m gonna marry ain’t born yet and her maw is dead.
Yeah, hurry up and do somethin’! I wants to taste a piece yo’ weddin’ cake.
Embarrassed but trying to be jocular.
Pointing to little man on porch.
Snaps his fingers and pretends to remember something.
He done moved so much since he been here till every time he walk out in his back yeard his chickens lay down and cross they legs.
Cody, I thought you tole us you was going up to Sanford to bring dat ’oman down here last Sat’day.
getting up and putting one hand on his hips and one finger of the other hand against his chin coquettishly
Gesture of kneeling on one knee and taking aim.
Supposedly sound of shots as the gun is moved in a circle following the course of Cody’s supposed flight.
I passed there and seen his house shakin’, but I didn’t know how come.
Aw, leave de boy alone.﻿ ﻿… If you don’t look out some of y’all going to have to break his record.
And I ain’t gonna leave Jim. We been palling around together ever since we hollered titty mama, ain’t we, boy?
Rabbit on the log. I ain’t got no dog. How am I gonna git him? God knows.
Rabbit on the log. Ain’t got no dog. Shoot him with my rifle Bam! Bam!
Bawls out from the store porch.
Well, Daisy, we knows you, too.
Gal, youse jus’ as pretty as a speckled pup.
Yeah, child, we’se been playin’ for the white folks all week. We’se playin’ for the colored now.
Showing off, twirling his dancing feet.
Um-ump, but they ain’t never workin’. Just round here playing as usual.
He sits back down on box and picks at his guitar.
Glad to be round home with we-all again, ain’t you Daisy?

Is I glad? I jus’ got off special early this evenin’ to come over here and see everybody. I was kinda ’fraid sundown would catch me ’fore I got round that lake. Don’t know how I’m gonna walk back to my workin’ place in the dark by muself.
Don’t no girl as good-lookin’ as you is have to go home by herself tonight.
I ain’t thinking ’bout goin’ home yet. I’m goin’ in the store.
What you want in the store?
Pulling package out of his pocket and laughing.
Yeah, there’s a lot of good parts to me. You can have West Tampa if you want it.
You always was a nice quiet boy, Jim.
Emerging from the store with a package of gum.
Oh, youse late. She’s done got gum now. Chaw that yourself.

I God, Lum, take your lazy self off that keg and go light that town lamp. All summer long you eatin’ up my melon, and all winter long you chawin’ up my cane. What you think this town is payin’ you for? Laying round here doin’ nothin’? Can’t you see it’s gettin’ dark?
Calling Dave, who is leaning against post at opposite end of porch.
Come on, sing a little, Dave.
“Got on the train, didn’t have no fare.”
The full melody of the guitar comes out in a lively, old-fashioned tune.
All right now, boys, do it for Daisy jus’ as good as you do for dem white folks over in Maitland.

Got on the train, Didn’t have no fare, But I rode some, I rode some. Got on the train, Didn’t have no fare, But I rode some, But I rode some. Got on the train, Didn’t have no fare, Conductor asked me what I’m doin’ there, But I rode some!

Grabbed me by the neck And led me to the door. But I rode some, But I rode some. Grabbed me by the neck And led me to the door. But I rode some, But I rode some. Grabbed me by the neck, And led me to the door. Rapped me cross the head with a forty-four, But I rode some.

First thing I saw in jail Was a pot of peas. But I rode some, But I rode some. First thing I saw in jail Was a pot of peas. But I rode some, But I rode some. The peas was good, The meat was fat, Fell in love with the chain gang jus’ for that, But I rode some.
I don’t blame them white folks for goin’ crazy ’bout that.﻿ ﻿…
Oh, when I was a young boy I used to swing the gals round on that piece.
Ha! Ha! Ol’ Dave’s gittin’ jealous when she speaks o’ Jim.
You oughta dance. Big as your feet is, Dave.
Pick a tune? I bet if you fool with me I’ll pick your bones jus’ like a buzzard did the rabbit. You can’t sing and now you wants to dance.
Yeah, and I’ll lam your head. Come on and play, good-for-nothing.
But I though you was playin’ for me now, Jim.
Sho, you ain’t stopped, is you, boy? Music sound mighty good floatin’ down that dark road.
Yeah, Jim, go on play a little more. Don’t get to acting so niggerish this evening.
Aw, let the ol’ darky alone. Nobody don’t want to hear him play, nohow. I know I don’t.
Look here, baby, at this new step I learned up North.
You can show me anything, sugar lump.
No, I ain’t jealous. I jus’ get tired of seein’ that ol’ nigger clownin’ all the time.
That’s just what I say. Niggers can’t have no fun without someone getting mad﻿ ﻿… specially over a woman.
I ain’t mad.﻿ ﻿… Daisy, ’scuse me, honey, but that fool, Dave.﻿ ﻿…
I ain’t mad neither.﻿ ﻿… Jim always tryin’ to throw off on me. But you can’t joke him.
You ain’t jokin’. You means that, nigger. And if you tryin’ to get hot, first thing, you can pull of my blue shirt you put on this morning.
Youse a got that wrong. I ain’t got on no shirt of yours.
Yes, you is got on my shirt, too. Don’t tell me you ain’t got on my shirt.
Well, even if I is, you can just lift your big plantations out of my shoes. You can just foot it home barefooted.
You try to take any shoes offa me!
Nobody’s quarreling.﻿ ﻿… I’m just playin’ a little for Daisy and Dave’s out there clownin’ with her.
Well, Mayor Clark, I ain’t mad with him. We’se been friends all our lives. He’s slept in my bed and wore my clothes and et my grub.﻿ ﻿…
I et your grub? And many time as you done laid down with your belly full of my grandma’s collard greens. You done et my meat and bread a whole lot more times than I et your stewed fish-heads.
Boys, boys, that ain’t no way for friends to carry on.

Well, if you all gonna keep up this quarrelin’ and carryin’ on I’m goin’ home. ’Bout time for me to be gittin’ back to my white folks anyhow. It’s dark now. I’m goin’, even if I have to go by myself. I shouldn’t a stopped by here nohow.
It may be so, I don’t know. But it sounds to me Like a lie.
Dave ain’t got as much rabbit blood as folks thought.
Ol’ fast Dave jus’ runnin’ the hog right over you, Jim.
Thought you was such a hot man.
Want me to go in there and put Daisy under arrest and bring her to you?
Sitting down on the edge of porch with one foot on the step and lights a cigarette pretending not to be bothered.
Stay off my foot, you big ox.
Well, you don’t have to wet me all up, do you, and me in company? Why don’t you put your damn foot in your pocket?

General hubbub, women’s cries of “Don’t let ’em fight.” “Why don’t somebody stop ’em?” “What kind of men is you all, sit there and let them boys fight like that.” Men’s voices urging the fight: “Aw, let ’em fight.” “Go for him, Dave.” “Slug him, Jim.”
Several men rush to the fallen man.
Run down to the pump and get a dipper o’ water.
Lock him up back yonder in my barn till Monday when we’ll have the trial in de Baptist Church.
Yeah, just like all the rest of them Methodists﻿ ﻿… always tryin’ to take undercurrents on people.
Ain’t no worse then some of you Baptists, nohow. You all don’t run this town. We got jus’ as much to say as you have.
Setting: Village street scene; huge oak tree upstage center; a house or two on backdrop. When curtain goes up, Sister Lucy Taylor is seen standing under the tree. She is painfully spelling it out.
Looks up at sun to tell time.
All men favors they guts, chile. But what you think of all dis mess they got goin’ on round here?
I just think it’s a sin an’ a shame befo’ de livin’ justice de way dese Baptis’ niggers is runnin’ round here carryin’ on.

Lawd help us! He can’t preach an’ he look like 10 cents worth of have-mercy let lone gittin’ up dere tryin’ to throw slams at us. Now all Elder Simms done wuz to explain to us our rights﻿ ﻿… whut you think ’bout Joe Clark runnin’ round here takin’ up for these ole Baptist niggers?
De puzzle-gut rascal﻿ ﻿… we oughter have him up in conference an’ put him out de Methdis’ faith. He don’t b’long in there﻿—wanter tun dat boy outa town for nothin’.
But we all know how come he so hot to law Jim outa town﻿—hit’s to dig de foundation out from under Elder Simms.
Whut he wants do dat for?
’Cause he wants to be a God-know-it-all an’ a God-do-it-all an’ Simms is de onliest one in this town whut will buck up to him.
Done got my clothes on de line an’ I’m bound to be dere.
Naw, I reckon﻿—don’t make such difference to me which way de drop fall.﻿ ﻿… ’Tain’t neither one of ’em much good.

Setting: A high stretch of railroad track thru a luxurious Florida forest. It is near sundown.

Action: When the curtain rises there is no one on the stage, but there is a tremendous noise and hubbub off stage right. There are yells of derision and shouts of anger. Part of the mob is trying to keep Jim in town, and part is driving him off. After a full minute of this, Jim enters with his guitar hanging around his neck and his coat over his shoulder. The sun is dropping low and red thru the forest. He is looking back angrily and shouting at the mob. A missile is thrown after him. Jim drops his coat and guitar and grabs up a piece of brick, and makes threatening gestures of throwing it.
Running back the way he came and hurling the brick with all his might.
Grabs up another piece of brick.
Threatens to throw again. There are some frightened screams and the mob is heard running back.
He puts on the shoe and looks back down the track again.

He sits there gloomily silent for awhile, then looks behind him and picks up his guitar and begins to pick a tune. The music is very sad, but he trails off into, “You May Leave An’ Go to Halimuhfacks, but My Slow Drag Will Bring You Back.” When he finishes he looks at the sun and picks up his coat.
Stops suddenly in his tracks and turns back toward the village. Takes a step or two.
